title: Education The Week the World Changed and the Classroom Changed a Little Stefan Bauschard
author: Bauschard, Stefan
summary: In the ten days of June 2-12, 2026, AI capability, adoption, and politics all lurched forward simultaneously while education mostly stood still. OpenAI and Anthropic both published foundational policy documents: Anthropic disclosed Claude now writes 90%+ of its own code and warned that fully recursive self-improvement 'could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for,' while also arguing for a verifiable global pause. Both companies simultaneously shipped the most capable models ever released publicly. Capital committed in 20-year horizons: SpaceX IPO'd at a $1.77 trillion valuation; OpenAI negotiated a 20-year lease on a half-trillion-dollar data center. ChatGPT hit one billion monthly users — the fastest app to that milestone in history. On the education side: 73% of K-12 teachers say AI will reshape education more than the internet did, but half say their students aren't using AI in class because it happens on phones, after the bell. Only five states require an AI policy. Sanders introduced a bill to nationalize 50% of AI companies; Trump mused about public equity. The labs wrote frameworks for Work and Live. Nobody wrote the one for Learn.
points: 'AI is arriving sooner than most institutions are prepared for' — Anthropic said this about itself, about a product it then shipped the same week it argued for a pause.
When two fierce commercial rivals both write down 'we may need to be stopped,' that is not marketing — that is a signal worth educators reading carefully.
OpenAI: 'Entirely automating everything is not the future we want... A key long-term role for people will be deciding what is worth doing' — a claim about what schools should be cultivating.
Capital is committing in 20-year horizons for a transition most school boards haven't planned through next semester.
The labs wrote frameworks for Work and Live. Nobody wrote the one for Learn — and that is the document that matters most.
quotes: I want to underline that Anthropic sentence, because it is, almost word for word, the thesis of this newsletter: AI is arriving sooner than most institutions are prepared for. The company building the thing said it about itself. Now apply it to schools.

OpenAI walked back its previous goal of a fully autonomous AI researcher, now framing that work as done 'in tandem' with humans, and added a line every educator should clip and tape to the wall: 'Entirely automating everything is not the future we want. It would be unfulfilling, and it would be dangerous... A key long-term role for people will be deciding what is worth doing.'
When two fierce commercial rivals both write down 'we may need to be stopped,' that is not marketing. That is a signal.
The people with the most money and the best information are planning in 20-year horizons for a transition most school boards haven't planned for through next semester.
The same institution arguing for a brake pedal spent the week demonstrating exactly why one might be needed.

Teachers see it — and feel unprepared. Nearly three in four K-12 teachers now say AI will reshape education more than the internet did. But half say their students aren't using it in class — because it's happening on phones, after the bell, where they can't see it.
The labs wrote frameworks for Work and Live. Nobody wrote the one for Learn — and that's the document that matters most.
